node.title: Re: Is A Number
node.author: kcott
node.doctext:
The suggested [https://perldoc.perl.org/Scalar::Util#looks_like_number|Scalar::Util::looks_like_number()] is often a good choice; however, be aware of some gotchas:

Infinity (see "[https://perldoc.perl.org/perldata#Special-floating-point:-infinity-(Inf)-and-not-a-number-(NaN)|perldata: Special floating point: infinity (Inf) and not-a-number (NaN)]"):

perl -E ' use Scalar::Util "looks_like_number"; for (qw{Inf -Inf Infinity -Infinity}) { say "$_: ", looks_like_number($_) ? 1 : 0; } ' Inf: 1 -Inf: 1 Infinity: 1 -Infinity: 1

Non-decimal numbers:

perl -E ' use Scalar::Util "looks_like_number"; for (qw{1 0b10 0o10 0x10}) { say "$_: ", looks_like_number($_) ? 1 : 0 } ' 1: 1 0b10: 0 0o10: 0 0x10: 0 perl -E ' use Scalar::Util "looks_like_number"; for (1, 0b10, 0o10, 0x10) { say "$_: ", looks_like_number($_) ? 1 : 0 } ' 1: 1 2: 1 8: 1 16: 1
"I would like to combine the string comparisons into as few as possible but seem to break the code every time I try."

If looks_like_number() is causing you problems, perhaps due to "gotchas" indicated above, or as a purely academic exercise, here's some hints for a hand-crafted solution.

Get rid of the blacklist: this will take ages to get right and, even then, there's a high chance that you'll miss an edge-case or two (or more). Just use a whitelist which represents valid numbers for your application.

Use a single regex with alternations, and only define it once (not in every iteration). With Perl v5.10 or higher, you can use this format:

sub IsNumber { state $re = qr{...}; return $_[0] =~ $re; }

For Perls of an older vintage:

{ my $re; BEGIN { $re = qr{...} } sub IsNumber { return $_[0] =~ $re; } }

Don't try to write your regex in the smallest possible space. This isn't a golfing exercise. Readability and maintainability will very quickly deteriorate. Use the /x modifier — or /xx if available; requires Perl v5.26 or later — as explained in "[https://perldoc.perl.org/perlre#/x-and-/xx|perlre: /x and /xx]".

Consider whether you're allowing exponents:

$ perl -E 'say 1e6' 1000000

What about when underscores have been used to improve the readability of large numbers:

$ perl -E 'say 1_000_000/1_000' 1000

Are you only dealing with 7-bit ASCII digits (/[0-9]/) or allowing the handling of all (i.e. Unicode®) digits (/\p{Digit}/)?

Note that /\d/ and /[[:digit:]]/ are not necessarily the same as /[0-9]/. See "[https://perldoc.perl.org/perlre#/a-(and-/aa)|perlre: /a (and /aa)]".

More general sources of reference are: [https://perldoc.perl.org/perlre|perlre]; [https://perldoc.perl.org/perlrebackslash|perlrebackslash]; and, [https://perldoc.perl.org/perlrecharclass|perlrecharclass].

— Ken
